blocks: This study addresses the quantification of dendritic evolution in coarsened microstructures. Such measurements stem from the computational assessment of a microstructure's interfacial orientations and curvatures. Samples of aluminum with 26% copper by weight (Al-26wt%-Cu) were coarsened for either 10 minutes or 5 days. Serial sectioning techniques were utilized in imaging and reconstructing the microstructures into three-dimensional arrays. Interactive Data Language (IDL) software was then employed to calculate the orientation and curvature from the triangulated three-dimensional surfaces. The data was finally displayed in Mean vs. Gaussian curvature and stereographically projected orientation probability density plots. Assessment of these distributions quantitatively illustrates a dendritic morphology toward a greater density of solid tubular shapes of low principle radii during coarsening.

One of the basic principles of materials science states that the overall behavior of a system is governed by the properties of its constituent parts. In this regard, the mechanical properties of metals are dictated by the microstructures formed during their solidification. A particular interest to a system's mechanical response is the substructure's component grain size and dendrite arm spacing. It has been experimentally demonstrated that as these parameters increase, the ultimate tensile strength and the percent elongation at fracture of the solidified metal decrease.¹ For this reason, grain size has been the traditional tool used to characterize a metal's mechanical properties. Flemings, however, has discovered that dendrite arm spacing yields a greater correlation to the mechanical responses.¹ Under this premise, it is proposed that understanding the evolution of these dendrites may be a significant step in quantifying the underlying processing-property relationship of solidified metals.

The above equations demonstrate that different compositions at the solid-liquid interface are a result of interfacial areas of differing curvature. In turn, these composition gradients lead to fluxes of solute through the dendrite, generating the morphological evolution of the solid-liquid mixture. A comprehension of the coarsening process will shed light on the morphology of the secondary arm spacing, which in turn divulges the morphological evolution of the entire dendritic microstructure. This morphology can be recounted by two basic assessments: the time evolution of interfacial orientations and surface curvatures. For such a detailed characterization, however, traditional two-dimensional microstructural information via metallographic cross-sections is insufficient. Instead, a three-dimensional analysis must be undertaken, and is described herein.

It is our objective to quantify the dendritic evolution in coarsened microstructures by generating three-dimensional reconstructions of dendritic microstructures. These digital reconstructions will then be analyzed for interfacial directionality and surface curvature variations. A range of coarsening times will be used to illustrate the evolution of the microstructure and to relate the subsequent microstructural array to the time-dependent coarsening process.
